To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

macular pigment optical densities (MPODs) are not significantly related to foveal short wavelength-sensitive (SWS)-cone mediated visual function, but are related to SWS-cone mediated visual function in the nasal visual field.
The relationship between macular pigment optical-density and SWS visual function was examined in the ageing eye using heterochromatic flickering photometry and orientation identification acuity.
the relationship between macular pigment optical densities and foveal and peripheral short-wavelength sensitive cone visual function was not significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the visual consequences of ageing in the normal human eye.
the role of the eye's natural filter, the macular pigment (MP), in protecting the retina from the damaging effects of short-wavelength light and in preserving foveolar SWS visual function.
the role of the macular pigment in the visual system, particularly with respect to its role in preserving fovea and parafovea short-wavelength (blue light) vision in the aging eye.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between fovea and 12° nasal visual field acuity with age is not significantly affected by macular pigment levels.
the role of macula pigment in preserving fwoveal SWS cone function with increasing age is not yet established.
the role of macula pigment in protecting foveal visual acuity in the ageing eye remains unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
macular pigment does not play a major role in protecting foveal short wavelength sensitive (SWS) cone visual function in the normal ageing eye.
macular pigment is not protective of foveal S-cone function in ageing eyes.
the role of macula lutea in preserving SWS visual function in the foveal region of the ageing eye is not supported.
The main takeaway from our work is that
macular pigment is unlikely to be the key factor in preserving fovea S-cone mediated visual function with age.
the macular pigment does not seem to be a protective factor against S-cone function decline in the foveal region.
the foveal and parafoveal retina are not equally affected by ageing.
